## Human Revision

### Statement

Consider the sequence $(a_n) = \left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)$. Prove that $(a_n)$ converges to $L = 1$.

### Solution

$\forall \varepsilon > 0$, $\exists N \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t. $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$, if $n > N$ then $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$.

Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Let $N = \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$.
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Suppose $n > N$. We compute
\begin{align*}
a_n &=  \frac{n+1}{n} \\
&=  \frac{n}{n} + \frac{1}{n} \\
&=  1 + \frac{1}{n}.
\end{align*}

<!-- > During a computation, you *always* start with only one thing. -->

We then subtract $1$ inside the absolute values and compute
\begin{align*}
\left|a_n -1\right| &= \left| 1 + \frac{1}{n} - 1\right|\\
&= \left| \frac{1}{n} \right|\\
&= \frac{1}{n}\\
&< \frac{1}{N} &\text{( $n> N$ means $\frac{1}{n} < \frac{1}{N}$.)}\\
&= \varepsilon.
\end{align*}

$\square$
